items.lead_agency: New York State Department of Environmental Conservation
items.description: Dutchess County - The New York State Department of Environmental Conservation, as lead agency, has determined that the proposed Clove Valley Rod and Gun Club Mine – 6.9 Acre Mine Expansion will not have a significant adverse environmental impact. The action involves the Clove Valley Rod & Gun Club Inc having an Article 23, Title 7 of the ECL Mined Land Reclamation permit to mine and process (dry screening only) sand and gravel from a maximum of 0.5 acres of a 9.47-acre total life of mine boundary area, situated on 2,950 acres controlled by the permittee. The permittee proposes to modify the mining permit to increase the size of the life of mine by 6.9 acres. The new expansion area would not be contiguous to the portion of the mine previously permitted. Expansion will allow for the excavation and removal of an estimated 142,000 cubic yards of sand and gravel and is expected to take 5 years. The expansion area would employ a minimum 200-foot setback from property boundaries, and a minimum 100-foot setback from NYS Freshwater Wetlands. The expansion area is proposed to be reclaimed as a 4.22-acre pond used for fishing. The project is located on North Clove Road in the Town of Union Vale, New York.

items.description: Erie County - The Hamburg Planning Board , as lead agency, has determined that the proposed 6433 Railroad Ave BESS Project may have a significant adverse impact on the environment and a Draft Environmental Impact Statement must be prepared. The action involves two co-located Tier 3 battery energy storage systems (BESS) in the Town of Hamburg, NY. The proposed system configuration includes five (5) units of the Tesla Megapack 2XL batteries, providing 4,896 kW capacity and 19,584 kWh energy delivery per project. Equipment is proposed to be mounted on a foundation pad and will include transformers, a meter, and switchgear. The project is located on an approximately 1.08-acre buildable area of a 2.7-acre site located at 6433 Railroad Avenue in the Town of Hamburg (Tax Map Parcel #193.00-4-2). items.title: Town of Busti - Water District Improvement Project
items.description: Chautauqua County - The Town of Busti, as lead agency, has determined that the proposed Town of Busti Water District Improvement Project will not have a significant adverse environmental impact. Currently, this portion of Town of Busti Water District No. 7 does not have municipal service, forcing all residential, commercial, and Town-owned facilities to rely on private groundwater wells. The Chautauqua County Department of Health strongly supports this project, noting that many local wells fail to meet NYSDOH standards due to recurring contamination and poor water quality. The action involves connecting the portion of Water District No. 7 to the Jamestown Board of Public Utilities (BPU) system. The project will also involve the installation of new water main, construction of a new water storage tank, and upgrades to an existing pump station. The project is located at Busti-Sugar Grove Road in the Town of Busti, New York.

items.title: City of Rome - 2026 Capital Improvement Project
items.description: Oneida County - The Rome City School District, as lead agency, has determined that the proposed 2026 Capital Improvement Project will not have a significant adverse environmental impact. The action involves the following: Staley Elementary School: Demolition of formerly-flooded school and other associated paved areas; and reseeding to cover area with grass. Clough Elementary School: Addition of approximately 16,000+/- sf to include a multipurpose space intended to function as gymnasium, cafeteria, and auditorium, Other portions of the addition will include a kitchen, locker rooms, offices, janitorial space, and event and gym equipment storage space. Connecting these new spaces to the existing building will be a new lobby and event entrance as well as a loading dock by the kitchen. There will also be approximately 6,000+/- sf of other interior renovations/reconfiguration to accommodate the proposed addition. The proposed new spaces will include a new library, new STEAM lab and counseling suite. The project will also include site work to accommodate the building addition and renovations. Rome Free Academy (RFA): Building and site work at the RFA Stadium Support Facility to include demolition of the existing grandstand and concession stand structure and construction of new stadium bleachers, stadium press box and associated site work. The project is located at Staley (former) Elementary School: 620 E Bloomfield Street; Clough Elementary School: 409 Bell Road; and Rome Free Academy Stadium Support Facility: 500 Turin Street in the City of Rome, New York.

items.description: Genesee County - The City of Batavia Planning and Development Committee, as lead agency, has made the Draft Scope for the proposed Baskin Livestock Processing Facility available. The Draft Scope is available at the following address: 1 Batavia City Center, Batavia, New York, 14020, and from the contact below online at: https://www.cityofbataviany.gov/m/newsflash/home/detail/76 . A public scoping session on the Draft Scope will be held on October 20, 2026 at 6:00 pm at 1 Batavia City Center, Batavia, New York, 14020. The action involves the rebuilding of an animal feed recycling facility that burned in November of 2024. The new facility will be an additional 8' away from Howard Street and will have a reduced footprint, with nearly 10,000 sq ft less of space under roof. The primary purpose of the scoping document is to outline the contents of the EIS and identify the impact analyses to be conducted. The project is located at 20 Howard Street in the City of Batavia, New York.

items.title: Statewide - Draft Finger Lakes Action Agenda 2026–2033
items.description: Draft Finger Lakes Action Agenda 2026–2033 Available for Public Comment The New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) announces the availability of the Draft Finger Lakes Action Agenda (FLAA) 2026–2033 for public comment. The FLAA is the first comprehensive regional strategic plan developed for the 11 Finger Lakes and their watersheds. The Finger Lakes combined watersheds encompass approximately 4,600 square miles across 12 counties in central and western New York. The plan was developed collaboratively by DEC’s Finger Lakes Watershed Program in partnership with a Steering Committee of state and federal agencies, academic institutions, nonprofit organizations, local governments, and community partners. The FLAA establishes six priority Goals and associated Objectives and Actions to guide the protection and restoration of water resources and ecological health across the Finger Lakes watershed through 2033: Goal 1: Reduce or Eliminate Toxic and Potentially Toxic Substances Goal 2: Control Sediment, Nutrient, and Pollutant Loadings Goal 3: Research, Monitor, and Manage Invasive Species Goal 4: Conserve and Enhance Fish and Aquatic Species and their Habitats Goal 5: Support Community Resilience and Ecosystem Integrity Goal 6: Protect and Enhance Recreation Access and Foster Sustainable Management The Draft FLAA is available for review on the DEC Finger Lakes Watershed Program webpage at: https://dec.ny.gov/nature/waterbodies/watersheds/management/great-lakes/finger-lakes-watershed A paper copy may be requested by contacting the DEC office listed below. Written comments on the Draft FLAA will be accepted through November 23, 2026 . Comments should be submitted to the contact listed below and must include “FLAA Comment” in the subject line.

items.project: Brownfield Cleanup Program (BCP) Application and Draft Remedial Investigation Work Plan from Shaw Building L.P. for a Site Known As C336103 - Shaw Factory Edward Street Site, Site ID #C336103
items.description: Fact Sheet The New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) has received a Brownfield Cleanup Program (BCP) application and Draft Remedial Investigation Work Plan from Shaw Building L.P. for a site known as C336103 - Shaw Factory Edward Street Site, site ID #C336103. This site is located in the City of Newburgh, within Orange County, and is located at 24-42 Johnes Street. Access the application and other relevant documents online through the DECinfo Locator: https://www.dec.ny.gov/data/DecDocs/C336103/ . The documents are also available at the document repository located at the Newburgh Free Library, 124 Grand Street, Newburgh, NY 12550. There are several ways to comment on BCP applications. Comments can be submitted to the Project Manager, Ryan Richard, NYS Department of Environmental Conservation, Division of Environmental Remediation, 21 South Putt Corners Road, New Paltz, NY 12561; via email to [email protected] ; or call (845) 256-3118. All comments must be submitted by November 20, 2026 . Site information can be viewed by entering the site ID noted above at: https://appfactory.dec.ny.gov/DERExternalSearch/ . We would also encourage those interested in receiving information on future activities at this site or any other site to sign up to DEC's Contaminated Sites Email List at: https://dec.ny.gov/environmental-protection/site-cleanup/regional-remediation-project-information/environmental-cleanup-email-newsletters What is the Brownfield Cleanup Program? New York’s Brownfield Cleanup Program (BCP) is designed to encourage private-sector cleanups of brownfields and to promote their redevelopment as a means to revitalize economically blighted communities. The BCP is an alternative to “greenfield” (land not previously developed or contaminated) development and is intended to remove some of the barriers to, and provide tax incentives for, the redevelopment of brownfields. Since its inception (2003), the BCP has catalyzed the cleanup of more than 500 contaminated sites statewide and incentivized redevelopment. There are more than 550 active sites in the BCP. Additional information on the State's Brownfield program is available at DEC’s website: https://dec.ny.gov/environmental-protection/site-cleanup/brownfield-and-state-superfund-programs/brownfield

The primary Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) representative of this facility is 2621 (Paper Mills Exc Building Paper), the secondary SICs are 2631 (Paperboard Mill), 2647 (Sanitary Paper Products), and 2676 (Sanitary Paper Products). The facility engages in the production of multiple paper products. items.title: Village of Pomona - Rockland County Riverway Trail
items.category: Notice of Acceptance of Final Environmental Impact Statement
items.lead_agency: Rockland County Department of Economic Development and Tourism
items.description: Rockland County - The Rockland County Department of Economic Development and Tourism, as lead agency, has accepted a Final Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) on the proposed Rockland County Riverway Trail. The Final EIS is available at the following address 50 Sanatorium Road Building A, 8th Floor Pomona, New York from the contact below and online at: https://www.rockland-riverwaytrail.com/resources . The action involves transforming and enhancing the existing major roadways, pedestrian, and non-motorized trails along the eastern side of Rockland County into a shared-use pedestrian and cycling network. This proposal does not include construction of any new trails or roadways. The Trail will cross through 10 different municipalities in the County and runs a total of approximately 21 linear miles. The Trail seeks to support the health and quality of life for County residents and visitors by creating a new outdoor recreation and transportation resource, enhancing opportunities for biking, walking, and jogging. The Trail will act as an engine for local economic development, tourism, and access to the County’s valuable open space amenities by introducing wayfinding signage. The Trail will provide convenient interconnection with various other regional trail networks as well. Where the Trail follows existing roadways, the project intends to improve safety and efficiency for both motorized and non-motorized transportation to better accommodate non-motorized users; this includes the repair, replacement, and/or construction of sidewalks, ramps, roadway striping, crosswalks, and shoulder extensions. It also includes the improvement of ancillary facilities to avoid impacts and to address existing issues from stormwater runoff. The project is broken down into a series of 11 segments, which will be constructed in 11 phases over an estimated 10-year time frame, depending on the availability of funding. The project is located in multiple Eastern Rockland County Municipalities at the Eastern portion of Rockland County, New York. The project is located at 50 Sanatorium Road Building A, 8th Floor in the Village of Pomona, New York.

items.title: New York City - Citywide Containerization Program
items.category: Notice of Acceptance of Final Environmental Impact Statement
items.lead_agency: New York City - The NYC Department of Sanitation (DSNY)
items.description: New York City - The NYC Department of Sanitation (DSNY), as lead agency, has accepted a Final Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) on the proposed Citywide Containerization Program. The Final EIS is available at the following address 125 Worth Street, Room 710 New York, New York, from the contact below and online at: https://www.nyc.gov/site/dsny/collection/containerization.page . The action involves DSNY proposing to implement a program to containerize waste at certain buildings with residential units and schools throughout the five (5) boroughs of New York City. Implementation of the Proposed Program would occur in phases with full Citywide implementation anticipated by 2032. Under the Proposed Program, buildings would containerize their refuse as follows for DSNY collection: (1) buildings with 10 to 30 residential units would have the option to use individual bins or stationery on-street containers; and (2) buildings with 31 or more residential units would use stationary on-street containers. Schools in Manhattan Community District (CD) 09 and Brooklyn CD 02 that receive DSNY collection services would utilize separate stationary on-street containers for each waste stream (refuse; organics; metal, glass, plastic, and cartons; and paper/cardboard). The use of stationary on-street containers and individual bins for waste disposal would allow DSNY to support the City’s commitment to street cleanliness and reducing potential food sources for vectors (e.g., rats and vermin). The Proposed Program seeks to improve municipal waste management practices to ensure safe and efficient waste collection, thereby reducing vector food sources and sightings while enhancing neighborhood character and street-side aesthetics in the City. The Proposed Program has been designed to account for varying building densities and operational needs, including conservative assumptions regarding storage capacity and collection frequency. The Proposed Program is intended to address longstanding issues associated with bagged waste, including sidewalk obstruction, litter, odors, worker safety, stormwater contamination, and attraction of vectors (e.g., rats and vermin). The Proposed Program would provide the following benefits: Eliminate the curbside placement of plastic bags containing refuse; Reduce potential food sources and/or attractants for rats and other vectors; Reduce litter, odor, loss of liquids and the potential contamination of stormwater runoff associated with plastic bags and the loss of materials from these; Reduce pedestrian and curbside obstructions; Contribute to improved public health; Reduce workplace injuries; Provide an overall improvement in street cleanliness and neighborhood aesthetics The project is located at 125 Worth Street, Room 710 in New York City, New York.

This is the first readoption of an Emergency Rulemaking that has been in effect since June 29, 2026. A Notice of Proposed Rulemaking with the same text was published in the July 15, 2026, New York State Register. This emergency rule is necessary for the preservation of the public health. ECL section 13-0307 requires that the Department examine shellfish lands and certify those that are in such sanitary condition that shellfish may be taken and used as food; all other lands must be designated as uncertified. Shellfish harvested from areas that do not meet the bacteriological standards for certified shellfish lands have an increased potential to cause illness in shellfish consumers. Closing areas that do not meet criteria for certified shellfish lands protects the public health. This rule will also open certain areas that now meet such criteria, update and clarify descriptions for enforcement purposes, reduce complexity, and improve readability of the regulations. This notice will be published in issue 41 of the State Register, dated October 14, 2026.

items.title: Statewide - 2010 Sulfur Dioxide National Ambient Air Quality Standard; August 2026
items.project: 2010 Sulfur Dioxide National Ambient Air Quality Standard; August 2026
items.description: 40 CFR 51.1205(b) Report; Albany, Bronx, Erie, Kings, New York, Niagara, Orange, Queens, Richmond, and Suffolk Counties; 2010 Sulfur Dioxide National Ambient Air Quality Standard; August 2026 Notice is hereby given that the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) plans to submit the above referenced report to the United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and is providing a 30-day period for the public to comment on the proposed report. On June 2, 2010, the EPA strengthened the primary (health based) sulfur dioxide (SO2) National Ambient Air Quality Standard (NAAQS) by establishing a new 1-hour standard at a level of 75 parts per billion (ppb). The EPA finalized the second round of designations for the 2010 primary SO2 NAAQS on July 12, 2016. In that final rule, the EPA designated the New York counties of Erie and Niagara as "unclassifiable/attainment" for the 2010 primary SO2 NAAQS based on an assessment and characterization of air quality performed using air dispersion modeling software, i.e., AERMOD, that analyzed actual emissions in the area surrounding Huntley (Erie County) and Somerset (Niagara County) generating stations, as well as other nearby sources which may have a potential impact in the area of analysis where maximum concentrations of SO2 are expected. The EPA finalized the third round of designations for the 2010 primary SO2 NAAQS on January 1, 2018. In that final rule, the EPA designated the New York counties of Albany, Orange, Suffolk, New York, Queens, Kings, Bronx, and Richmond as "unclassifiable/attainment" for the 2010 primary SO2 NAAQS based on an assessment and characterization of air quality in the area surrounding Lafarge Building Materials (Albany County), Roseton Generating Station (Orange County), Northport Power Station (Suffolk County), and several power stations in the New York City area. Pursuant to 40 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) 51.1205(b), "[f]or any area where modeling of actual SO2 emissions serve as the basis for designating such area as attainment for the 2010 SO2 NAAQS, the air agency shall submit an annual report to the US EPA Regional Administrator ... that documents the annual SO2 emissions of each applicable source in each such area and provides an assessment of the cause of any emissions increase from the previous year." DEC plans to submit "40 CFR 51.1205(b) Report; Albany, Bronx, Erie, Kings, New York, Niagara, Orange, Queens, Richmond, and Suffolk Counties; 2010 Sulfur Dioxide National Ambient Air Quality Standard; August 2026" to the EPA. The final report satisfies the requirements of 40 CFR 51.1205(b) for 2026 by demonstrating that all counties included in the report continue to attain the 2010 SO2 NAAQS by a significant margin and that no additional air quality modeling is needed. The proposed report can be requested from the contact listed below. Written comments should be submitted by 5:00 p.m. on November 13, 2026, to the contact listed below.

items.description: New York County - The New York City Department of Parks and Recreation, as lead agency, has determined that the proposed 79th Street Boat Basin Reconstruction Project will not have a significant adverse environmental impact. The action involves protecting and restoring coastal resources at the 79th Street Boat Basin, a NYC Parks facility that has been closed since November 2021 due to safety concerns associated with substantial deterioration. In coordination with the New York City Economic Development Corporation, NYC Parks would reconstruct the boat basin to improve marina resiliency, upgrade utilities to current standards, provide full compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), and increase public access to slips. The proposed work would include reconstruction of the deteriorated wharf; establishment of a new design elevation that incorporates sea level rise projections; and integration of the reconstructed structure with the adjacent upland area of Riverside Park. items.title: City of Elmira - Elmira Sewer District Green Infrastructure
items.description: Chemung County - The Chemung County Sewer Districts, as lead agency, has determined that the proposed Elmira Sewer District Green Infrastructure will not have a significant adverse environmental impact. The Chemung County Sewer Districts (CCSD) owns and maintains the Elmira Sewer District which consists of a combined sewer system that conveys both stormwater and wastewater. This combined sewer system regularly experiences combined sewer overflow events during precipitation events. The action involves an urban & suburban redevelopment project incorporating “green” stormwater practices in the downtown areas of Elmira within the Railroad Ave and College Ave sewer sheds, which are two of the most active sewer sheds within the Elmira Sewer District. Chemung County Sewer District has received funding to implement the first phase of a green infrastructure program, which is expected to consist of multiple phases over multiple years. The first phase is expected to consist of pavement narrowing, installation of tree trenches and tree pits, and the replacement of impervious on-street parking with pervious paver parking. It is CCSD’s goal to further reduce the frequency of combined sewer overflow events across the Elmira Sewer District and from these particular sewer sheds. As such, it is anticipated this project will be the first of many green infrastructure redevelopment projects that will occur within the CCSD Railroad & College Ave ‘A’ Green Infrastructure Project Area. This SEQR review is intended to cover both the currently planned phase of the green infrastructure program and a larger project area where future green infrastructure phases will be constructed over the next several years. Conducting this environmental review across the larger project area will allow the project team to select specific project areas within the larger boundary that will minimize environmental, social, and historical impacts. The project is located throughout in the City of Elmira, New York.

items.title: Brooklyn - Revised Brooklyn-Queens Expressway/Interstate 278 (“BQE”) from Atlantic Avenue to Nassau Street Project (BQE Central Project)
items.project: Revised Brooklyn-Queens Expressway/Interstate 278 (“BQE”) from Atlantic Avenue to Nassau Street Project (BQE Central Project)
items.category: Positive Declaration, Availability of Draft Scope and Public Scoping Session
items.lead_agency: New York City Department of Transportation (NYC DOT)
items.description: Kings County - The New York City Department of Transportation (NYC DOT), as lead agency, has determined that the proposed Brooklyn-Queens Expressway/Interstate 278 (“BQE”) from Atlantic Avenue to Nassau Street Project (BQE Central Project) may have a significant adverse impact on the environment and a Draft Environmental Impact Statement must be prepared. The Draft Scope is available at the following address, from the contact below and online at: https://www.nyc.gov/html/dot/html/infrastructure/bqecentral.shtml . This notice has been revised from a previous notice that has been retracted and replaced by the following. The Draft Scope is available from the contact listed below and online at: www.nyc.gov/bqe . An in-person public scoping session will be held on November 10, 2026 from 6:30 PM to 8:30 PM at New York City College of Technology, 300 Jay Street, Brooklyn, New York. A virtual public scoping session will be held on November 12, 2026 from 6:30 PM to 8:30 PM via Zoom. Information on how to join and comment is available at www.nyc.gov/bqe . Written comments on the Draft Scope will be accepted through November 23, 2026. NYC DOT is proposing the rehabilitation of the BQE from Atlantic Avenue to Nassau Street, in the Borough of Brooklyn. The purpose of the Project is to address identified structural deficiencies of BQE Central and maintain the regional vehicular connectivity and mobility that the highway provides. The action involves an approximately 1.5-mile section of the BQE from just north of Atlantic Avenue to Nassau Street. The project limits include the BQE Central roadway, shoulders and offsets, support structures, Furman Street, the Brooklyn Heights Promenade, local street overpasses and underpasses between Atlantic Avenue and Nassau Street, and adjacent New York City-owned property, including parking lots, maintenance and storage areas, and open space. Within the project limits, the BQE parallels the eastern and southern shore of the East River through a densely developed urban area, with a wide range of land uses in proximity to the project limits. BQE Central includes the unique 0.4-mile-long triple cantilever section. The structure takes advantage of an extreme change in elevation between the Brooklyn waterfront and Brooklyn Heights. It is composed of two levels of highway and the Brooklyn Heights Promenade on a structure elevated above Furman Street. The structure hangs from a retaining wall that extends from ground level to the top of the bluff. The cantilever section begins at Joralemon Street just north of Atlantic Avenue and ends at Washington Street. The Project would involve a major rehabilitation of all 21 structures within the project limits to address structural deficiencies and increase their service life. The New York State Historic Preservation Office (SHPO) has determined the portion of the BQE between Brooklyn Heights and the Kosciuszko Bridge to be eligible for listing on the State and National Registers of Historic Places (S/NR-eligible). In addition, the Brooklyn Heights Promenade is within the Brooklyn Heights Historic District, which the New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission (LPC) has designated a New York City Landmark district; the district is also S/NR-listed. The Project would generally retain the historic integrity of the highway within the project limits, including the triple cantilever structure. NYC DOT would replace the superstructure of the Columbia Heights overpass and relocate and reconstruct its north abutment. NYC DOT would rehabilitate all the other bridges and structures within the project limits to extend their service life. At the triple cantilever section, the Project would maintain the existing mainline and ramp alignments, lane widths, shoulder widths, horizontal and vertical clearances, and other roadway geometric features. With the Project, BQE Central would continue to operate as it does today, with two lanes in each direction except for a short section of the highway between the Manhattan Bridge and just south of Sands Street which operates with three full lanes in the Staten Island-bound direction only. East of Adams Street, NYC DOT would explore addressing non-standard features where practicable. The Project would correct current drainage issues and would provide a new bridge railing that meets current design standards. The project limits include a portion of the property at 25 Joralemon Street. NYC DOT would acquire the portion of the property that is vacant and encased within the existing BQE structure. NYC DOT would not acquire the occupied portion of this structure that is immediately east of the BQE. The project limits also include small sections of mapped parkland adjacent to the roadway, which NYC DOT would incorporate through alienation legislation by the New York State legislature, including a home rule action by the New York City Council. The Project would require City Map amendments to account for these alterations to land use. To fully rehabilitate the structure, NYC DOT would construct two temporary bypass structures alongside the current highway that would carry traffic during construction. One bypass structure would parallel the triple cantilever section from just north of Atlantic Avenue to Columbia Heights; this structure would be located within the Furman Street right-of-way below the promenade elevation. A second bypass structure would carry traffic from Columbia Heights, potentially above the Brooklyn Bridge, and through Dumbo, tying back into the highway structure just west of the Manhattan Bridge. Upon the completion of construction, NYC DOT would demolish both temporary structures. NYC DOT anticipates that construction would commence in 2029 and would be completed before 2040. NYC DOT continues to develop the construction means and methods for the Project. As part of these efforts, NYC DOT will explore innovations aimed at shortening the duration of construction. The project is located at Brooklyn-Queens Expressway/Interstate 278 (“BQE”) from Atlantic Avenue to Nassau Street in Brooklyn, New York.

items.project: Green Resiliency Grant (GRG) Program – $45 Million Available
items.description: Green Resiliency Grant (GRG) Program – $45 Million Available The Environmental Facilities Corporation (EFC) will offer grants for eligible projects that improve water quality and mitigate the effects of extreme weather through the Green Resiliency Grant (GRG) program. This grant funding is made available through the Clean Water, Clean Air and Green Jobs Environmental Bond Act of 2022 (Bond Act). GRG awards are made on a competitive basis to transformative stormwater management projects that protect homes, businesses, and public infrastructure throughout New York State while advancing long-term community resilience. Eligible projects combine green and gray infrastructure for holistic stormwater solutions that effectively and sustainably (1) manage runoff from extreme weather events to reduce flood risk and improve water quality; and (2) prioritize community resilience and equitable access to ensure infrastructure investments provide reliable benefits to all residents, particularly vulnerable populations. The GRG program may fund up to 90 percent of eligible project costs with grants ranging from a minimum of $1 million to a maximum of $10 million per project. Eligible applicants include Municipalities and State Entities as defined by NYS Environmental Conservation Law Article 58. Additional information on the GRG program, including the Program Summary, can be found on EFC’s website at: https://www.efc.ny.gov/GRG .

New York’s Brownfield Cleanup Program (BCP) is designed to encourage private-sector cleanups of brownfields and to promote their redevelopment as a means to revitalize economically blighted communities. What is the Brownfield Cleanup Program? New York’s Brownfield Cleanup Program (BCP) is designed to encourage private-sector cleanups of brownfields and to promote their redevelopment as a means to revitalize economically blighted communities. The BCP is an alternative to “greenfield” (land not previously developed or contaminated) development and is intended to remove some of the barriers to, and provide tax incentives for, the redevelopment of brownfields. Since its inception (2003), the BCP has catalyzed the cleanup of more than 500 contaminated sites statewide and incentivized redevelopment. There are more than 550 active sites in the BCP. items.title: Brooklyn - Brooklyn-Queens Expressway/Interstate 278 (“BQE”) from Atlantic Avenue to Nassau Street Project (BQE Central Project)
items.project: Brooklyn-Queens Expressway/Interstate 278 (“BQE”) from Atlantic Avenue to Nassau Street Project (BQE Central Project)
items.category: Positive Declaration, Availability of Draft Scope and Public Scoping Session
items.lead_agency: New York City Department of Transportation (NYC DOT)
items.description: Kings County - The New York City Department of Transportation (NYC DOT), as lead agency, has determined that the proposed Brooklyn-Queens Expressway/Interstate 278 (“BQE”) from Atlantic Avenue to Nassau Street Project (“BQE Central” or the “Project”) may have a significant adverse impact on the environment and a Draft Environmental Impact Statement must be prepared. The Draft Scope is available from the contact listed below and online at: www.nyc.gov/bqe . An in-person public scoping session will be held on November 4, 2026 from 6:30 PM to 8:30 PM at Saint Francis College, 179 Livingston Street, Brooklyn, New York. A virtual public scoping session will be held on November 5, 2026 from 6:30 PM to 8:30 PM via Zoom. Information on how to join and comment is available at www.nyc.gov/bqe . Written comments on the Draft Scope will be accepted through November 16, 2026. NYC DOT is proposing the rehabilitation of the BQE from Atlantic Avenue to Nassau Street, in the Borough of Brooklyn. The purpose of the Project is to address identified structural deficiencies of BQE Central and maintain the regional vehicular connectivity and mobility that the highway provides. The Project involves an approximately 1.5-mile section of the BQE from just north of Atlantic Avenue to Nassau Street. The project limits include the BQE Central roadway, shoulders and offsets, support structures, Furman Street, the Brooklyn Heights Promenade, local street overpasses and underpasses between Atlantic Avenue and Nassau Street, and adjacent New York City-owned property, including parking lots, maintenance and storage areas, and open space. Within the project limits, the BQE parallels the eastern and southern shore of the East River through a densely developed urban area, with a wide range of land uses in proximity to the project limits. BQE Central includes the unique 0.4-mile-long triple cantilever section. The structure takes advantage of an extreme change in elevation between the Brooklyn waterfront and Brooklyn Heights. It is composed of two levels of highway and the Brooklyn Heights Promenade on a structure elevated above Furman Street. The structure hangs from a retaining wall that extends from ground level to the top of the bluff. The cantilever section begins at Joralemon Street just north of Atlantic Avenue and ends at Washington Street. The Project would involve a major rehabilitation of all 21 structures within the project limits to address structural deficiencies and increase their service life. The New York State Historic Preservation Office (SHPO) has determined the portion of the BQE between Brooklyn Heights and the Kosciuszko Bridge to be eligible for listing on the State and National Registers of Historic Places (S/NR-eligible). In addition, the Brooklyn Heights Promenade is within the Brooklyn Heights Historic District, which the New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission (LPC) has designated a New York City Landmark district; the district is also S/NR-listed. The Project would generally retain the historic integrity of the highway within the project limits, including the triple cantilever structure. NYC DOT would replace the superstructure of the Columbia Heights overpass and relocate and reconstruct its north abutment. NYC DOT would rehabilitate all the other bridges and structures within the project limits to extend their service life. At the triple cantilever section, the Project would maintain the existing mainline and ramp alignments, lane widths, shoulder widths, horizontal and vertical clearances, and other roadway geometric features. With the Project, BQE Central would continue to operate as it does today, with two lanes in each direction except for a short section of the highway between the Manhattan Bridge and just south of Sands Street which operates with three full lanes in the Staten Island-bound direction only. East of Adams Street, NYC DOT would explore addressing non-standard features where practicable. The Project would correct current drainage issues and would provide a new bridge railing that meets current design standards. The project limits include a portion of the property at 25 Joralemon Street. NYC DOT would acquire the portion of the property that is vacant and encased within the existing BQE structure. NYC DOT would not acquire the occupied portion of this structure that is immediately east of the BQE. The project limits also include small sections of mapped parkland adjacent to the roadway, which NYC DOT would incorporate through alienation legislation by the New York State legislature, including a home rule action by the New York City Council. The Project would require City Map amendments to account for these alterations to land use. To fully rehabilitate the structure, NYC DOT would construct two temporary bypass structures alongside the current highway that would carry traffic during construction. One bypass structure would parallel the triple cantilever section from just north of Atlantic Avenue to Columbia Heights; this structure would be located within the Furman Street right-of-way below the promenade elevation. A second bypass structure would carry traffic from Columbia Heights, potentially above the Brooklyn Bridge, and through Dumbo, tying back into the highway structure just west of the Manhattan Bridge. Upon the completion of construction, NYC DOT would demolish both temporary structures. NYC DOT anticipates that construction would commence in 2029 and would be completed before 2040. NYC DOT continues to develop the construction means and methods for the Project. As part of these efforts, NYC DOT will explore innovations aimed at shortening the duration of construction.

items.description: Fact Sheet The New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (NYS DEC) has received a Brownfield Cleanup Program (BCP) application from 80 Richards Street LLC for a site known as Former Atlas White Metals Co. Site, site ID #C224238. This site is in the Borough of Brooklyn, within the County of Kings and is located at 235-237 Van Brunt Street, 67-69 Delavan Street, and 76 Verona Street. Access the application and other relevant documents online through the DECinfo Locator: https://extapps.dec.ny.gov/data/DecDocs/C224238/ . The documents also are available at the document repositories located at the Brooklyn Public Library – Red Hook Branch, 362 Van Brunt Street, Brooklyn, NY 11231; and at the Brooklyn Community Board 6, 250 Baltic Street, Brooklyn, NY 11231. There are several ways to comment on BCP applications and work plans. Comments can be submitted to the site Project Manager Wendi Zheng at NYS Department of Environmental Conservation, Division of Environmental Remediation, 1 Hunter’s Point Plaza, 47-40 21 st Street, Long Island City, NY 11101; via email at [email protected] or by calling (718) 482-7541. All comments must be submitted by October 30, 2026 . Site information can be viewed by entering the site ID noted above at: https://appfactory.dec.ny.gov/DERExternalSearch/ We would also encourage those interested in receiving information on future activities at this site or any other site to sign up to DEC's Contaminated Sites Email List at: https://dec.ny.gov/environmental-protection/site-cleanup/regional-remediation-project-information/environmental-cleanup-email-newsletters. What is the Brownfield Cleanup Program? New York’s Brownfield Cleanup Program (BCP) is designed to encourage private-sector cleanups of brownfields and to promote their redevelopment as a means to revitalize economically blighted communities. The BCP is an alternative to “greenfield” (land not previously developed or contaminated) development and is intended to remove some of the barriers to, and provide tax incentives for, the redevelopment of brownfields. Since its inception (2003), the BCP has catalyzed the cleanup of more than 500 contaminated sites statewide and incentivized redevelopment. There are more than 550 active sites in the BCP. Additional information on the New York State's Brownfield program is available at NYS DEC’s website: https://dec.ny.gov/environmental-protection/site-cleanup/brownfield-and-state-superfund-programs/brownfield

items.title: Town of Seneca Falls - West Bayard Street Culvert Maintenance Project - Amended 2026
items.project: West Bayard Street Culvert Maintenance Project - Amended 2026
items.lead_agency: Town of Seneca Falls Town Board
items.description: Seneca County - The Town of Seneca Falls Town Board, as lead agency, has determined that the proposed West Bayard Street Culvert Maintenance Project - Amended 2026 will not have a significant adverse environmental impact. The action involves the complete maintenance and repairs on an existing stone arch culvert and repairing a timber cribbing spill inlet box. The culvert and inlet box are partially full of debris. The culvert is missing motor and stone and there is visible soil and void spaces. The inlet box has damaged and missing timbers. The project involves slip-lining an existing stone arch culvert and repairing a timber cribbing spill inlet box. Material that has been deposited in the culvert will be removed, which consists of typical sedimentation of silts, sands, gravel, stones, organics and vegetation. The project has since been amended as follows: The project no longer involves slip-lining the existing stone arch culvert and repairing a timber cribbing spill inlet box, but rather demolition the existing culvert and inlet structure and constructing a new 8 ft by 8 ft concrete culvert and new concrete inlet structure. Material that has been deposited in the culvert will be removed, which consists of typical sedimentation of silts, sands, gravel, stones, organics and vegetation. An area of approximately 30 feet by 30 feet around the inlet box will be dredged. No dredging is expected to be done on the canal side. Dredged material will be hauled off-site to a landfill or approved upland location. Temporary coffer dams will be constructed in the pond and in the canal so the maintenance work can be completed in the dry. The coffer dams will likely be of Portadam type and watertight sheet piling. The level of the canal may be lowered 5 to 8 feet to lessen the height of the coffer dams. Work can be completed from the top of the pond headwall and canal wall. Some work may be performed in the pond between the coffer dam and headwall, in the area of dredging. The project is located at 31-29 W Bayard Street in the Town of Seneca Falls, New York.

What is the Brownfield Cleanup Program? New York’s Brownfield Cleanup Program (BCP) is designed to encourage private-sector cleanups of brownfields and to promote their redevelopment as a means to revitalize economically blighted communities. The BCP is an alternative to “greenfield” (land not previously developed or contaminated) development and is intended to remove some of the barriers to, and provide tax incentives for, the redevelopment of brownfields. Since its inception (2003), the BCP has catalyzed the cleanup of more than 500 contaminated sites statewide and incentivized redevelopment. There are more than 550 active sites in the BCP. The BCP is an alternative to “greenfield” (land not previously developed or contaminated) development and is intended to remove some of the barriers to, and provide tax incentives for, the redevelopment of brownfields. Since its inception (2003), the BCP has catalyzed the cleanup of more than 500 contaminated sites statewide and incentivized redevelopment. There are more than 550 active sites in the BCP. Additional information on the New York State's Brownfield program is available at NYS DEC’s website: https://dec.ny.gov/environmental-protection/site-cleanup/brownfield-and-state-superfund-programs/brownfield

items.title: Statewide - Treatment of Hemlock (Tsuga canadensis) Trees to Protect against Hemlock Woolly Adelgid (Adelges tsugae) on NYS Wildlife Management Areas
items.project: Treatment of Hemlock (Tsuga canadensis) Trees to Protect against Hemlock Woolly Adelgid (Adelges tsugae) on NYS Wildlife Management Areas
items.lead_agency: Statewide - The New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (NYS DEC)
items.description: Statewide - The New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (NYS DEC), as lead agency, has determined that the proposed Treatment of Eastern Hemlock (Tsuga canadensis) Trees to Protect against Hemlock Woolly Adelgid (Adelges tsugae) on NYS Wildlife Management Areas will not have a significant adverse environmental impact. The NYS DEC Bureau of Wildlife proposes to treat hemlock with insecticides (dinotefuran and/or imidacloprid) to protect them from hemlock woolly adelgid (HWA), an invasive forest insect pest that was introduced from China, in select areas on the NYS Wildlife Management Areas (WMA) system, which encompasses approximately 250,000 acres across almost 150 sites statewide. The proposed insecticide application is intended to kill hemlock woolly adelgid (HWA), which has spread across much of New York State by wind, birds and the movement of infested host material (firewood, nursery stock, etc.). Left untreated, HWA causes needle loss, decline in health and eventually death of hemlock trees. Hemlock is a critical native tree species in New York as it provides soil stabilization and protects water quality, particularly in steep ravines, gullies and other headwater riparian corridors. Furthermore, hemlock provides important habitat for plants and animals and aesthetic value. Hemlock is a significant component of more than 22,000 forested acres on NY’s WMA system. The proposed action would consist of the annual treatment of hemlock with insecticides to kill HWA on up to 2,200 acres (<1% of the total WMA system acreage) of upland forest on the WMA system. Insecticide applications will be ongoing and could require repeat treatment of individual trees every 5 to 10 years. Treatments will be in accordance with the insecticide product label, which has undergone extensive review and approval by NYS DEC Bureau of Pesticide Management as part of the registration process. New York has successfully completed multiple HWA treatments across NY on WMAs, State Forests, Forest Preserve lands, and State Parks over the past 15 years without any documented adverse environmental impacts. Protecting hemlock trees has important ecological benefits and preserves valuables ecosystem services. In reaching this determination, DEC considered the following information: • The proposed action involves the targeted application of specific insecticides in accordance with the product labels has been reviewed by DEC's Bureau of Pesticides Management and approved for use in New York. Treatments must carefully comply with label requirements regarding application rates to minimize runoff or accumulation. Specifically, basal bark treatments will only occur at periods of low wind to avoid drift toward nearby waterways and will use calibrated equipment to prevent overspray that runs off onto the soil. Insecticide soil tablets will not be used within 75 feet of waterways. Research suggests that soil drench applications of Imidacloprid (the technique most likely to result in pesticide movement to waterways) do not have negative effects on nearby aquatic macroinvertebrate communities. Techniques to be used for this action have an even lower risk of entering waterway than the studied soil drench. • The proposed action involves the use of insecticides to control a damaging, invasive insect, thus, there is risk that non-target invertebrates may be affected. However, the proposed treatment methods result in the systemic uptake of the applied insecticides, meaning the insecticides are not broadcast into the environment and only kill insects that eat the treated plant. Hemlocks are pollinated by wind (not bees, etc.) therefore there will be no impact on pollinator species. Basal bark treatment avoids any insecticide being absorbed by non-target plants. Tablets will only be used under pure stands of hemlock so the insecticide cannot be taken up by the roots of nearby flowering plants. Native insects that feed on hemlocks may be impacted; however, their populations would likely be severely impacted by widespread hemlock death, so long-term survival of hemlocks on the landscape (goal of project) will benefit them, even if there is individual losses from this treatment. Only a selection of hemlock per acre will be treated each year; most hemlock trees within a stand will remain untreated, so non-target population impacts are not expected. • The proposed action overlaps with some areas designated as sensitive for archaeological sites; however, because the action does not involve construction or other ground disturbing activities, it will not impact cultural resources or other resources such as wildlife habitat or significant ecological communities. Insecticide applications are completed by trained applicators, typically on foot using backpack sprayers with calibrated application equipment. • The proposed action is located on public recreation lands and during the actual treatments, temporary signs will be placed to keep the public away from the specific treatment sites for 24 hours. This impact to public use is extremely minimal and far outweighed by the habitat conservation benefits. • The proposed action can only be undertaken under the supervision of New York State-certified pesticide applicators or technicians. All applications must follow the product labels' instructions for PPE and safety and all applicable regulations. Basal bark treatments will be applied during periods of little to no wind (0-10 mph) to minimize risk of non-target impacts from spray drift and no precipitation for 12-hour window before and after treatment. • The proposed action does not involve insecticide treatments in or around surface waters or in NYS-regulated wetlands or adjacent areas. For HWA treatments in those areas, DEC will obtain state permits that include a separate, individual SEQRA review. • The proposed action will have no adverse impacts to state or federally-listed threatened and endangered species or their habitats. Because the insecticide application is ground-based and non-broadcast (application to the bark or via tablet), no protected insect species will be affected. If this action is not undertaken, hemlock mortality is likely to expand, resulting in negative effects to NY’s ecosystems, wildlife habitat, aesthetics, and public use of Wildlife Management Areas. The long-term goal of insecticide treatments is to keep a component of hemlocks alive long enough for biological control agents to become established across NY. The project is located in multiple locations in the state of New York.

items.project: Notice of Proposed 2027 Atlantic Ocean Surfclam Annual Harvest Limit
items.description: Public Comment Period for Notice of Proposed 2027 Atlantic Ocean Surfclam Annual Harvest Limit Pursuant to Environmental Conservation Law Section 13-0309 and Subpart 43-2 of Title 6 of the New York Codes, Rules and Regulations, the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (Department) hereby gives notice of the following: The Department is proposing to establish the 2027 annual harvest limit for surfclams taken by mechanical means from the certified areas of the Atlantic Ocean at 184,558 industry standard bushels, which would maintain the level of harvest (total allowable catch) that was established from 2016 to 2026. The number of vessels harvesting surfclams from the Atlantic Ocean and the percentage of the annual harvest limit taken by the surfclam fishery has been steadily declining. The level of harvest is low enough that the Department does not see a need to reduce the annual harvest limit. Without more recent surfclam population and resource information, maintaining the annual harvest limit is necessary to protect the long-term sustainability of the resource and economic viability of the surfclam fishery. The Department will announce the annual harvest limit for 2027 no later than November 15, 2026, with an effective date of January 1, 2027, after taking into consideration public comment and any other relevant fishery related information. Written comments on the proposed 2027 Atlantic Ocean surfclam annual harvest limit will be accepted by mail, email, or fax until close of business Thursday, October 1, 2026.

This site is in the City of Yonkers, within the County of Westchester and is located at 372 Riverdale Avenue and 13 Culver Street. What is the Brownfield Cleanup Program? New York’s Brownfield Cleanup Program (BCP) is designed to encourage private-sector cleanups of brownfields and to promote their redevelopment as a means to revitalize economically blighted communities. The BCP is an alternative to “greenfield” (land not previously developed or contaminated) development and is intended to remove some of the barriers to, and provide tax incentives for, the redevelopment of brownfields. Since its inception (2003), the BCP has catalyzed the cleanup of more than 500 contaminated sites statewide and incentivized redevelopment. There are more than 550 active sites in the BCP. items.title: Town of Huntington - Ruland Road Substation Expansion and Reactor Installation
items.project: Ruland Road Substation Expansion and Reactor Installation
items.description: Suffolk County - The Long Island Power Authority (LIPA), as lead agency, has determined that the proposed Ruland Road Substation Expansion and Reactor Installation will not have a significant adverse environmental impact. The action involves the expansion of the existing Ruland Road Substation (the “Substation”) for the installation of new Substation equipment on LIPA property on the north side of Ruland Road in Melville. The project also includes reconfiguration of two existing transmission circuits entering the Substation from the southwest, including transmission tower removals and transmission pole installations and replacements. The project will provide additional electrical capacity and flexibility for the LIPA electric system and will support the delivery of energy from Long Island to the rest of New York State to meet state energy goals. The Substation will be expanded by approximately 0.38 acres to the west onto vegetated LIPA-owned land. The expansion area will be cleared of vegetation and regraded and new perimeter fencing with access gates will be installed. New Substation equipment and support structures will be installed within the expansion area, including six 138kV Air Core Reactors, four new A-frame structures for incoming transmission lines, two 138kV gang-operated disconnect switches, and associated bus work. Crushed stone will be installed on the ground surface of the expansion area. The new equipment will range in height from approximately 24 feet above grade to 65 feet above grade. Several evergreen trees will be installed along the southern fenceline of the Substation along Ruland Road. Two existing overhead transmission circuits currently enter the Substation from the southwest and will require reconfiguration to accommodate the new equipment installations. All pole work will be located on LIPA property, either within the existing Substation or to the immediate southwest. Two lattice steel transmission towers, at heights of approximately 115 feet and 90 feet above grade, respectively, will be removed and will be replaced with six steel transmission poles, at heights between approximately 70 and 125 feet above grade. One wood transmission pole at a height of approximately 45.5 feet above grade will be replaced by a wood transmission pole at a height of approximately 57 feet above grade. One new wood transmission pole at a height of approximately 52 feet above grade will be installed. One wood transmission pole at a height of approximately 45.5 feet above grade will be replaced with a wood transmission pole at a height of approximately 59 feet above grade and relocated approximately 135 feet to the southwest of the existing pole location. In total, the project will require a total of approximately 0.56 acres of ground disturbance, of which approximately 0.53 acres will be within pervious soil or vegetated areas, and approximately 0.02 acres will be within the existing dolomite-covered Substation. The project is located adjacent to the existing Ruland Road Substation on Ruland Road in Melville in the Town of Huntington, New York.

items.title: Towns of Riverhead, Southampton, and Southold - SCWA North Fork Water Main Extensions: Riverside/Flanders to Southold Town line and East Marion to Orient Village
items.project: SCWA North Fork Water Main Extensions: Riverside/Flanders to Southold Town line and East Marion to Orient Village
items.description: Suffolk County Water Authority (SCWA) is the sponsor for a proposed project, which would extend a new watermain from a suitable and reliable source of drinking water from SCWA’s South Shore Low pressure zone (part of which is within Long Island’s deep recharge area through a connection in Flanders) to the Town of Southold. The purpose of the project is to improve water supply to the existing service area (Phase 1) as well as a future long-range planning for a possible future water main extension between East Marion and Orient in the Town of Southold (Phase 2). The project would serve residential and non-residential premises in the Hamlet of Orient that are currently experiencing private well contamination issues. The water main extension would involve the installation of a water main from the intersection of Flanders Road and Cross River Drive in the Town of Southampton to the Riverhead-Southold Town line (Phase 1) and from the west side of Dam Pond in East Marion to Orient Village in Southold (Phase 2). The DEIS examines three possible routes for the proposed transmission main to get to Southold with particular emphasis on what are identified as the Proposed Action (Cross River Drive to Northville Turnpike to Sound Avenue to the Riverhead-Southold Town line) and Preferred Alternative (Cross River Drive to Main Road to the Riverhead-Southold Town line). One route was identified for the East Marion to Orient extension. The DEIS weighs the benefits and potential impacts of the identified options and provides project mitigations to prevent or mitigate impacts to the maximum extent practicable, and ensure a safe and sustainable source of water to SCWA’s Southold system. Public hearings were held on the DEIS on August 19, 2026, August 20, 2026 and August 26, 2026 and the written comment period was scheduled to close on September 15, 2026. To ensure that the public and involved and interested agencies have plenty of time to review and comment on the DEIS, SCWA has extended the written comment period to September 25, 2026 at 5:00 PM. The DEIS is available for review online at SCWA’s official website at: https://www.scwa.com/nfp/ or in paper copy at the following four locations: Suffolk County Water Authority Westhampton Building 624 Old Riverhead Road, Westhampton Beach, NY 11978 M-F 9:00 AM to 4:00 PM Southold Free Library 53705 Main Road, Southold, NY 11971 M-F 9:30 AM to 8:00 PM Sat 9:30 AM – 5:00 PM Riverhead Public Library 330 Court Street Riverhead, NY 11901 M-Th 9:00 AM to 8:00 PM F-Sat 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM Town of Riverhead Town Hall 4 West Second Street Riverhead, NY 11901 M-F 8:30 AM – 4:30 PM Send all correspondence by September 25, 2026 at 5:00 PM to:

items.project: Notice of Proposed Rulemaking - Part 151 Propagation of Furbearing Animals
items.description: Notice of Proposed Rulemaking - Part 151 Propagation of Furbearing Animals Pursuant to the Environmental Conservation Law sections 3-0301, 11-0303, 11-1907, the Department of Environmental Conservation hereby gives notice of the following: Notice of Proposed Rulemaking to repeal 6 NYCRR Part 151 pertaining to propagation of fur-bearing animals. In March 2012, Environmental Conservation Law section 11-1907 was amended, prohibiting the Department from issuing any new licenses for propagation of fur-bearing animals. Individuals who possessed a current license as of April 1, 2012, could continue licensing providing they renewed their license annually. The last license issued pursuant to this section expired December 2021, therefore rendering the regulation obsolete. This notice will be published in issue 36 of the State Register, dated September 9, 2026.

items.title: Town of Rotterdam - Schenectady - C Well Field
items.applicant: CITY OF SCHENECTADY 105 JAY ST SCHENECTADY, NY 12305 Facility : SCHENECTADY - C WELL FIELD 20 RICE RD ROTTERDAM, NY 12305
items.permits: Article 15 Title 15 Water Withdrawal Public
items.description: The applicant proposes to withdraw 35,000,000 gallons per day of water for use in the City of Schenectady water supply and distribution system, increasing the well capacity by approximately 15%. This includes the installation of three new groundwater wells, three new prefabricated steel well house buildings, yard piping, meter vaults and site improvements. This action will also consolidate and supersede all previous Water Withdrawal permits issued to the City of Schenectady.

items.permits: Article 15 Title 5 Dam
items.description: New York City Department of Environmental Protection (NYCDEP) proposes to create an interim notch approximately 4.5 feet deep and 60 feet wide in the spillway of the Ashokan Dam (State ID 193-0855). In addition, a scour protection blanket will be installed upstream and baffles constructed immediately downstream. The project will be located at the Ashokan Reservoir East Basin Spillway in the Town of Marbletown, Ulster County.
